item.title: Singer Asif Akbar’s car targeted by gunfire in Moghbazar: Police
item.description:
Gunmen fired at singer Asif Akbar’s private car in Moghbazar, the capital, on Saturday morning. He was not in the vehicle at the time of the incident.

The incident took place in front of Bishal Centre in Moghbazar at around 5:30 am on Saturday. Mohammad Asaduzzaman, officer-in-charge (OC) of Hatirjheel police station, confirmed the information.

Prothom Alo contacted Asif Akbar by mobile phone at around 9:00 am to ask about the incident, but he did not respond.

Asaduzzaman told Prothom Alo, “Asif Akbar has a personal office in Moghbazar. His private car was parked in front of Bishal Centre. Early in the morning, one or more unidentified individuals arrived, fired shots at the car and fled. No one was injured or killed in the incident.”

The OC said the police had yet to determine who fired the shots or what motivated the attack.

He added that the police were collecting CCTV (closed-circuit television) footage from cameras in the surrounding area to identify those involved.

Hatirjheel police station said it would take the necessary legal action over the incident.

item.title: Markets, malls return to previous schedule of 11am to 8pm
item.description:
Markets, shopping malls and shops across the capital will remain open from 11:00 am to 8:00 pm following the expiry of the temporary extension of shopping hours during Durga Puja.

Under a directive issued by the Power Division on 5 October, the city's markets, shopping malls and shops were allowed to remain open until 10:00 pm during the festival. The extended schedule remained in effect until Thursday.

The previous schedule came into effect again on 23 October, according to the directive.

On 12 August, the government imposed restrictions on shopping hours as part of its efforts to save and manage electricity.

The Power Division also instructed shops and shopping malls to switch off lights after 7:00 pm.

item.title: Marco Rubio calls on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with CIA
item.description:
USA-RUBIO/INDIA

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on those seeking change in Cuba to partner with the CIA as President Donald Trump said Washington would "take care of Cuba" after dealing with Iran and send in the top US diplomat to finish the deal.

Details and quotes:

  • "We'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran ... then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump told a rally in Florida.

  • "To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time," Rubio, who has been handling much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump, said on X on Friday.

  • Rubio urged those disappointed by Cuba's government to "seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA," without elaborating further.

  • The Trump administration has previously stated its goal is to change Cuba's communist government.

  • A US-imposed ⁠oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put Cuba under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

  • Washington has maintained an embargo on Cuba for over 60 years.

  • The Trump administration has been stepping up pressure on Havana after the US military in January seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a deadly raid.

  • Cuba's foreign minister told the UN General Assembly last month Cuba would always be open for dialogue with Washington.

  • UN rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights advocates say the Trump administration's threats have echoed an imperialist approach.

  • Trump predicted last month the US and Cuba would reach an agreement and that he did not think military action would be necessary.

item.title: BRT project cancellation: Are politicians the only ones to blame?
item.description:
Political governments come and go, but those who certify project feasibility remain. Holding them accountable would be the real measure of development. Who should be held responsible for the cancellation of the BRT project? In this article, Subail bin Alam seeks to find the answer.

On 18 October, the Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, decided to cancel the Airport–Gazipur Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project. The stations and lane dividers will be dismantled, turning the corridor into an ordinary highway.

When the project was approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) in 2012, its estimated cost was around Tk 20.4 billion. It was supposed to be completed in 2016. After three revisions, the cost rose to Tk 42.68 billion. In 2025, ECNEC under the interim government rejected a proposal seeking a further increase to Tk 65.98 billion in the fourth revision. By then, Tk 28.11 billion had already been spent, yet not a single dedicated bus had taken to the road.

The project was financed primarily through foreign loans. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) approved a loan of $260 million, while the French Development Agency provided a loan of €40 million. Even though the project has been cancelled, the disbursed loans must still be repaid with interest. Yet I have been unable to find figures showing how much of the approved financing was actually disbursed.

The human cost is even greater than the financial loss. Seven people died in various accidents during construction. On 15 August 2022, five members of the same family were killed in Uttara when a concrete girder fell on them. At the time, this writer published an article on the subject on Prothom Alo’s website. But nothing changed.

Through my professional work, I have had the opportunity to work on almost all of the country’s mega-projects, including this BRT project. Time and again, I witnessed unsafe construction practices, faulty planning, and internal theft. Even repeated warnings about safety failed to get through to the Chinese contractor. Today, we are all paying the price for those mistakes.

A team of experts from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) found that even if the BRT had become operational, passengers travelling from Gazipur would still have had to get off at the airport and change buses. Moreover, the specially designed buses, with doors on the right-hand side, could not have operated outside the dedicated corridor.

However, cancelling the project also comes at a cost. According to the Bangladesh Institute of Planners, dismantling the infrastructure and restoring the corridor could require more than another Tk 10 billion.
Three questions must therefore be considered separately: Was the decision to cancel the project justified? How much will cancellation cost? And who is responsible for 14 years of failure? The Cabinet has answered the first question, but no one has spoken up about the third.
BRT is not an exception, but part of a pattern

A white paper committee reviewed seven major projects undertaken by the previous Awami League government and found that their costs had been increased from Tk 1.14 trillion to Tk 1.95 trillion without cost-benefit analyses. The committee estimated that, out of approximately $60 billion allocated to development projects over 15 years, between $14 billion and $24 billion had been squandered through bribery, extortion, theft, and inflated budgets.

In the first year of operation, traffic forecasts for the Karnaphuli Tunnel projected 18,485 vehicles per day. In reality, an average of just 3,910 vehicles used it daily. Figures presented by the Roads and Bridges Minister in Parliament in June 2026 showed that monthly toll revenue still stood at Tk 33.7 million, while expenses amounted to Tk 69.5 million. We do not know who prepared this forecast, which was off by nearly a factor of five, who reviewed it, or who signed it off.

There are rules in place, after all. Feasibility studies are mandatory for government projects costing more than Tk 500 million. Yet RAJUK submitted a proposal worth Tk 168 billion without conducting a feasibility study. I have repeatedly warned about the Ganges Barrage project as well: proceeding to the main contract on the basis of an outdated 2013 feasibility study would repeat the same mistakes. The paperwork that enables rules to be violated is prepared right at officials’ desks.

BRT: 14 years of misery, Tk 30b spent, only for the project to be cancelled

Six signatures before ECNEC

ECNEC decides which projects to approve; it is the technical professionals who certify whether a project is feasible. The BRT project was approved before its comprehensive feasibility study and design had been completed. Once construction began, it became apparent that there was no drainage system, no plan to relocate utility lines, and no alternative traffic arrangements for the busy roads.

At least six levels of scrutiny failed to catch these shortcomings:
1. The consultants responsible for the feasibility study and design.
2. The implementing agency and the project director.
3. The ministry secretary.
4. The Planning Commission and the Project Evaluation Committee, which also approved three rounds of revisions.
5. The Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED).
6. The financiers: the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the French Development Agency.

BUET described the project as a systemic failure and recommended ensuring accountability for the consultants and officials involved. ECNEC under the interim government had also called for those responsible to be identified. Yet no reports have emerged of action being taken against anyone. On the contrary, following the deaths of five people in Uttara in 2022, the Roads and Highways Department’s own investigation committee blamed the Chinese contractor and declared that the project authorities had played no role. The department effectively absolved itself of responsibility.

According to Professor AK Enamul Haque, a member of the white paper committee, bureaucrats plundered 40 per cent of the Annual Development Programme (ADP) funds over 15 years. A consultant whose feasibility study is proven wrong generally faces no obstacles in bidding for subsequent projects. A project director under whose watch costs double rarely has their promotion held up. The personal cost of failure is virtually zero, so behaviour remains unchanged.

How other countries hold signatories accountable

United Kingdom: The permanent secretary of each ministry is personally accountable to Parliament for public spending as the “accounting officer.” If an expenditure fails to meet even one of the following criteria—regularity, propriety, value for money, or feasibility—the secretary must seek a written directive from the minister. That directive is made public, and responsibility shifts to the minister.

In 2016, despite written objections from the transport secretary over London’s Garden Bridge project, the minister issued a directive and assumed responsibility for an additional £15 million in spending. The project was eventually cancelled, resulting in a loss of £43 million in public funds. However, the records clearly identify who raised objections and who overrode them by issuing the directive.

South Korea: Since 1999, an independent institution, the Korea Development Institute (KDI), rather than individual ministries, has conducted preliminary feasibility studies for major projects. Before that, between 1994 and 1998, the ministries’ own feasibility studies had approved 32 out of 33 projects. According to South Korean estimates, reviewing 961 projects between 1999 and 2022 generated development-related savings of approximately 170 trillion won.

However, there is also a cautionary lesson here: exemptions and relaxed criteria introduced in the name of regional development caused the approval rate for projects outside the capital to jump from 52 percent to 89 percent. This brings our own “fast-track” projects to mind.

World Bank: In connection with the Padma Bridge project in 2013, the World Bank debarred SNC-Lavalin for 10 years. In 2023, it debarred the local consulting firm BETS for 22 months over payments made by the firm to officials in connection with a water project in Chattogram. The power to blacklist firms exists, but the punishment comes from the lender rather than from our own public procurement system.

Chain of accountability: Six proposals

However, accountability does not mean indiscriminate punishment. Incorrect forecasts, negligence, and deliberate corruption are not the same thing. Delays in land acquisition, slow fund disbursement, and pressure from superiors can also be genuine problems. That is precisely why a system of written objections is needed, so that the distinction between reasonable risks and knowingly made mistakes is documented on paper.

Let the process begin with the BRT project. An independent committee outside the ministry should determine within 90 days who signed off on which feasibility studies, designs, or revisions, and who ignored which warnings. Its report should be made public, identifying individuals by name and specifying their roles. Confidentiality cannot be used as an excuse when public money has been wasted.

The next step is structural reform:

Independent review agency: An institution independent of the ministries, modeled on the Korea Development Institute (KDI), should review feasibility studies for projects costing more than Tk 500 million. Its reports should be submitted to Parliament. No exemptions should be allowed for “fast-track” projects.

Written certifications to be submitted to parliament: Under a Development Project Proposal (DPP), the secretary and project director should sign certifications confirming that a project is feasible and implementable. If a minister overrides their professional judgment, the minister must issue a written directive. Both documents should be submitted to the Public Accounts Committee and the Comptroller and Auditor General. Major projects should also be subject to a public hearing once a year.

Financial liability for consultants: Professional liability insurance and performance bonds should be made mandatory. When seeking compensation from BRT contractors, the cost of defects arising from faulty designs should also be recovered from the consultants. Furthermore, if a multilateral development bank debars anyone, that person should automatically become ineligible to work on public projects in Bangladesh as well.

Automatic postmortem review: An independent review should be conducted whenever a project’s cost increases by more than 20 percent or it undergoes a second revision. The costs, progress, forecasts, and actual outcomes of every major project should be published on a single website. If there is evidence of corruption, the case should be referred to the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC).

Project directors should be engineers: Technical mega-projects should be led by full-time engineers with relevant experience in the sector. They should be assigned to the projects for their entire duration. The position must not become a reward for someone’s promotion.

A Chief Technical Officer in the Prime Minister’s Office: Engineers are responsible for carrying out nearly 70 percent of the work under the Annual Development Programme (ADP), yet they have little role in decision-making. The government also has to rely on bureaucrats’ advice to move projects forward. To address this weakness, an engineer could be appointed as a Chief Technical Officer (CTO) in the Prime Minister’s Office. The CTO would provide technical advice to the government and ensure proper oversight of major projects.

Generating revenue from what has already been Built

Loan repayments will continue regardless. Leaving completed assets unused would therefore amount to a second waste of public money. Where demand exists but management is weak, toll-operate-transfer agreements could be awarded through open tenders.

In 2018, India leased out nine operational highways for 30 years, receiving an upfront payment of 96.81 billion rupees—1.5 times its own estimate. This means transferring operational responsibility, not ownership.
Where demand can be generated, as in the case of the Karnaphuli Tunnel, the Anwara economic zone must be brought into operation quickly. The tunnel’s daily operating costs have been reduced from Tk 3.7 million to Tk 2.2–2.3 million. This indicates that the earlier costs had been inflated.

Where demand does not exist, the objective should be to minimize losses.
The lifts, escalators, and steel structures at the BRT’s 15 stations should undergo an independent valuation and then be sold through open auction or reused in other projects. Demolition work must also be awarded through transparent tenders. Otherwise, the cancellation process itself could become a new avenue for plunder.

In addition, following Professor Shamsul Hoque’s recommendation, a commuter train service between Gazipur and Kamalapur should be introduced using the railway’s third and fourth tracks.

Governments change, but the signatories remain

For 14 years, the people of Gazipur have endured dust and traffic congestion, and seven people have lost their lives. If all they get in return is a cancellation letter, with not even a single line written naming those who signed off on the project, then the foundation for the next BRT failure is being laid today.

Announcing the cancellation of a project does not end the responsibility. The government must also disclose how public money was wasted and provide answers.

Political governments come and go, but those who certify project feasibility remain. Holding them accountable would be the real measure of development.

item.title: Shipbreaking industry sees 150 workers killed in 12 years
item.description:
There was a time when Reshma Akter did not have to worry about household expenses. Her father, Mohammad Munsur, supported the family by working at a shipbreaking yard. But on 14 August, 21-year-old Reshma lost her father. Now, there is no one in the family who earns a living.

Reshma, who has completed higher secondary education, is also unemployed. She spends her days worrying about how the family will survive.

Reshma Akter is from Moulvipara of Bhatiari area in Sitakunda upazila of Chattogram. Her father, Munsur, 55, was one of the 10 workers who died from toxic gas at Ferdous Steel Ship Recycling Industries. When they heard about the accident, Reshma and her family rushed to the factory. But they could not see her father. By then, he was being taken to hospital. They buried him that night.

The family has kept the Tk 1 million they received as compensation in savings, hoping to draw some money from it every month. But Reshma worries whether that will be enough to run the household. She laments, “My father is gone!”

Reshma's family is not alone. Over more than a decade, more than a hundred families have lost loved ones in accidents at shipbreaking yards in Sitakunda. Many others have suffered serious injuries and fallen into financial hardship.

Government inspections, accident records and research have repeatedly highlighted safety shortcomings. Yet workers continue to dismantle ships while putting their lives at risk.

When asked, Tapan Dutta, convener of the Shipbreaking Workers Trade Union Forum, told Prothom Alo that although laws exist to ensure workers' safety, they are not properly enforced. Accidents continue because the necessary protective equipment and training are not ensured.

Another family devastated

Sani Das, 20, an assistant worker, also died in the same accident at Ferdous Steel. His elder brother, Liton Das, 25, used to work at a garment factory. However, he lost his job because he could not regularly attend work while arranging his brother's last rites and other related matters. He previously earned Tk 14,000 to Tk 15,000 a month. Now he is unemployed.

After Sani's death, their mother, Asra Bala Das, returned to work at a garment factory to support the family. She earns around Tk 13,500 a month. According to Liton, his mother's health has also deteriorated since her son's death. Her monthly medicine expenses range from Tk 1,000 to Tk 1,500.

The family received Tk 1 million in compensation. After various expenses, Tk 500,000 to Tk 600,000 remains. Liton said, “We are now living on loans. I don't have a job either. My mother has started working at a garment factory again.”

150 workers killed in 12 years

At least 150 workers were killed and at least 264 injured in accidents at shipbreaking yards in Sitakunda over the 12 years from 2015 to mid-October 2026.

These figures were obtained through an analysis of records maintained by the Bangladesh Institute of Labour Studies (BILS), a labour research organisation.

According to BILS, 16 workers died in 2015, 18 in 2016, 19 in 2017, 13 in 2018 and a record 23 in 2019. Subsequently, 10 workers died in 2020, 13 in 2021, seven each in 2022, 2023 and 2024, and four in 2025. Three workers died in the first six months of the current year, while another 10 died at Ferdous Steel in August.

Similar accidents have been occurring at different yards year after year. In 2017, Khalilur Rahman died after falling from a height at Ferdous Steel. In 2018, Borhan Uddin was killed when struck by an iron plate at Premium Trade Corporation. The following year, three workers died in an explosion and fire at the same factory, while another three died from toxic gas at MAC Corporation.

In 2022, Md Faruk died while cutting a ship at HM Shipbreaking. In 2024, six workers were killed in an explosion and fire at SN Corporation.

The suffering of injured workers is no less severe. In 2019, worker Hiralal suffered a spinal fracture in an accident at MAC Corporation. In the same year, the flesh on worker Md Nasir's leg was torn away after he was struck by a heavy piece of iron at Janata Steel.

There is no comprehensive record of how many injured workers have recovered and returned to work or permanently lost their ability to work.

Dipu Das, who survived the accident at Ferdous Steel, said, “I had to receive treatment in hospital for three days. But I still haven't recovered from the trauma of the accident.”

Mohammad Mohsin Chowdhury, president of the Bangladesh Ship Breakers and Recyclers Association (BSBRA), the leading organisation of shipbreaking industry owners, told Prothom Alo that initiatives had been taken to formulate new safety guidelines and establish training centres for workers following the accidents.

Nature of risks remains unchanged

Of the 28 accidents documented by BILS in the first six months of the current year, nine involved workers being struck by heavy iron and machinery. Eight involved injuries caused by cranes, hooks and cables, while five involved gas and fire. Of the 25 injured workers, 10 sustained serious injuries.

A study on the risks of shipbreaking was published in the Open Journal of Safety Science and Technology on 18 June. The researchers collected information from 1,074 workers and supervisors at 18 shipbreaking yards.

The study identified 105 types of potential hazards associated with shipbreaking activities. These included 17 types of hazards in iron-cutting work, 14 in the removal of hazardous materials, and 12 each in dismantling machinery and removing oil waste. The researchers recommended regular training, protective equipment, supervision and the maintenance of accident records.

Md Mahbubul Hasan, deputy inspector general of the Department of Inspection for Factories and Establishments (DIFE) in Chattogram, told Prothom Alo that government agencies lacked the capacity to oversee such a complex industry. Nevertheless, two to three yards are inspected every month. Notices are issued and cases filed when irregularities are found. Three cases have also been filed against Ferdous Steel.

Safety concerns persist despite green certification

According to the industry owners' association, 23 shipbreaking yards currently hold green certification. Ferdous Steel is also among the certified yards.

However, the Department of Inspection for Factories and Establishments had found safety shortcomings at the yard six months before the accident. Following a notice, a case was filed with the Labour Court in July. The following month, 10 workers died.

An investigation by the Ministry of Industries also found serious negligence. Necessary protective equipment was not used for hazardous work. Although work continued on a holiday, there was no safety manager, physician or emergency rescue team. The investigation also found that a ship's tank had been declared safe without proper inspection.

item.title: Messi receives Spain’s top sports honour from Princess Leonor, heir to the throne
item.description:
SPAIN-ROYALS/AWARDS

Lionel Messi received Spain's most prestigious sports award on Friday in recognition of his glittering career and his work for disadvantaged children's access to health and education.

The Argentine forward, 39, was named winner of the Princess of Asturias Award for Sports in June, with the jury hailing "the most successful footballer of all time" and his social work.

Dozens of fans wearing Argentina football shirts cheered and chanted Messi's name as he arrived to the sound of bagpipes and drums at the ceremony in Oviedo, capital of the northern Spanish region of Asturias.

Messi collected a formal roll of parchment from Princess Leonor, the heir to the Spanish throne after whom the awards are named, who lauded his "unique career".

"He turned the extraordinary into routine by reading the game and deciding on the most effective option in fractions of a second, while respecting the collective essence above ego," Leonor said.

One of the greatest footballers of all time, Messi has won eight Ballon d'Or titles, a World Cup and dozens of trophies at club level.

He spent 21 years at Barcelona where he played in a side that dominated Spain and Europe under Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique.

After leaving the Catalan club in 2021, Messi spent two years at French giants Paris Saint-Germain and currently plays for Inter Miami in MLS.

Argentina's all-time top goalscorer, assist provider and caps holder called time on his international career earlier this year after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey.

"The most important thing is to know how to lose and how to win," Messi told an event with children in Oviedo on Thursday, saying that attitude was "fundamental" in football.

Founded in 1981, the Princess of Asturias Awards are the most prestigious in the Spanish-speaking world and come with prize money of 50,000 euros ($56,000).

They encompass the arts, sciences and sports and are handed out annually in honour of efforts to improve human coexistence, solidarity and global cooperation.

British author Julian Barnes, trailblazing US astronaut Christina Koch and punk star Patti Smith were among the other winners who received their prize on Friday.

Previous winners of the sports award include tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal, marathon record-breaker Eliud Kipchoge and US skier Lindsey Vonn.

item.title: Concessions for shipbreaking put environment and workers at risk
item.description:
The shipbreaking industry is considered one of the most polluting industries for the environment. Therefore, businesses must obtain approval at several stages, including conducting an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), before setting up a yard.

However, the government has decided to downgrade the industry from the red category to the orange category, meeting a long-standing demand from shipbreaking yard owners. This decision could remove the requirement to conduct an EIA before establishing a yard.

Entrepreneurs in the shipbreaking industry say that, because the industry falls under the red category, it takes around 90 days to obtain approval to set up a yard. They claim that this delay causes them financial losses.

Environmentalists, however, fear that the government’s decision will put both workers and the environment at risk. They say shipbreaking is a high-risk and highly polluting industry.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) has described it as one of the most dangerous industries. Marine ecosystems, soil and air along the coastlines of Chattogram and other South Asian areas where shipbreaking takes place are suffering severe pollution.

According to sources, the committee responsible for the matter decided on 29 September to reclassify the industry from the red category to the orange category.

The Prime Minister’s Office formed the committee in August to review existing laws, regulations, policies and related matters concerning the ship recycling industry.

Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo chairs the committee. The industry minister, the state minister for shipping, the Cabinet Secretary, the Finance Division Secretary, and the Law and Parliamentary Affairs Secretary are its members. However, the committee includes no representatives from environmental organisations or environmental experts.

Asked about the decision, Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo told Prothom Alo, “We have 15 to 20 green yards under the Hong Kong Convention.”

According to business owners, they have invested around Tk 1.5 billion (150 crore) in each yard. As the shipbreaking industry falls under the red category, they have to wait three months to obtain permission to establish a yard. This delay is causing financial losses for businesses.

Asked whether the government’s decision would increase the risk of environmental pollution, he said, “We must protect both the environment and the industry.”

Under the Environment Conservation Rules 2023, both shipbreaking activities and shipbreaking yards fall under the red category. The rules state that factories or establishments in the red category have severe impacts on the environment and human health. Significant measures are therefore necessary to address these impacts.

What do the existing rules say and what is set to change?

Under the existing rules, anyone seeking to establish a shipbreaking yard must first conduct an environmental impact assessment (EIA). The requirement also applies to the shipbreaking industries of India and Pakistan.

Currently, a yard must submit detailed terms of reference (ToR), outlining the measures it will take to prevent pollution, to the Department of Environment’s headquarters and obtain approval before beginning the EIA process.

As part of the process, a representative of the Department of Environment leads a public consultation in the relevant area. The representative then sends a report containing the feedback received to the department’s district office. The department’s headquarters reviews the report once again before issuing a site clearance certificate for the proposed yard.

The next step is obtaining an environmental clearance certificate. The department issues this certificate after inspecting the measures taken by the yard to prevent pollution from harming the environment and human health. The entire process takes 90 days.

If the government reclassifies the shipbreaking industry under the orange category, these requirements will no longer apply in the same way. Under the Environment Conservation Rules 2023, industries in the orange category must submit an initial environmental examination report to the divisional office of the Department of Environment.

If the divisional office considers an EIA necessary, it may recommend one. However, the yard will not be obliged to follow that recommendation. Applicants will no longer need to approach the department’s headquarters for final approval to establish a yard; the divisional office will issue the approval.

Several officials at the Department of Environment told Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity that the changes to the rules would prevent the authorities from assessing how much pollution a yard might cause and the extent of its environmental impact. They warned that the monitoring system for the industry would become weaker.

Abdun Naser Khan, secretary of the Ministry of Industries, told Prothom Alo, “This is a highly promising industry. By 2030, around 6,500 ships worldwide will be ready for scrapping. If we can increase the number of green yards, we will secure a substantial share of the shipbreaking business.”

According to sources at the Department of Environment, shipbreaking yards in Sitakunda, Chattogram, currently dismantle 150 to 200 ships every year. It takes six months to dismantle a single ship. Between 30,000 and 35,000 workers are employed at these yards.

Environmental experts say that shipbreaking must comply with the Basel Convention, under which each party must take responsibility for its own waste. If ships carrying waste from developed countries arrive in Bangladesh, the developed countries must remain responsible for that waste.

They argue that dry docks — specialised facilities designed for ship repair and dismantling — are the only viable option for shipbreaking in Bangladesh.

The industry cannot become environmentally friendly simply by laying concrete on open sea beaches. They stress that strict compliance with all relevant national and international laws are essential to make the industry safe.

Syeda Rizwana Hasan, chief executive of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), told Prothom Alo that relaxing the rules contradicted ongoing litigation concerning shipbreaking pollution, as well as court judgments and orders. She added that the government had not informed the court before making the decision.

“Ten workers died from gas emissions as recently as August. This kind of decision will put workers’ lives at even greater risk,” she said.

Rizwana Hasan added, “During the fascist regime, we saw industries being permitted to set up inside the Ecologically Critical Area of the Sundarbans with a single stroke of the pen. It is unacceptable for the elected government to make decisions in this manner.”

She questioned why the government had not invited any environmental experts or activists before making such a major decision on shipbreaking, when it had consulted environmentalists while making decisions concerning Saint Martin’s Island.

item.title: Blockade enforced in Rangamati and Khagrachhari
item.description:
A half-day blockade of road and waterways has been underway in the hill districts of Khagrachhari and Rangamati since early Saturday. The programme was called by an organisation named the Chhatra-Janatar Sangram Parishad (Students-People's Struggle Council). The blockade is scheduled to continue until noon today.

The organisation said the programme was being observed in protest against attacks, beatings and vandalism of homes and shops during the road blockade in Sajek, and in solidarity with the demands of Sajek residents.

Road transport along the Rangamati-Khagrachhari highway has been suspended due to the blockade. No long-distance buses have left Khagrachhari. However, traffic on the Rangamati-Chattogram highway remains normal. Protesters have staged demonstrations by burning tyres at various locations in the two districts. In some places, they have placed tree trunks and felled trees to block roads.

According to local sources, traffic on internal roads in Rangamati city, including those in the Banarupa and Kalyanpur market areas, remains normal. Long-distance vehicles have also been seen operating on the Rangamati-Chattogram highway.

Meanwhile, protesters have been picketing by placing tree trunks and setting fires on the Rangamati-Khagrachhari highway in the Sapsari Khamarpara and Kutukchhari Dharmaghar areas. A protest procession was also held from Kutukchhari Half Bazar to Dharmaghar.

Mohammad Selim, a CNG-run autorickshaw driver on the Rangamati-Chattogram highway, told Prothom Alo, "Traffic on the Rangamati-Chattogram highway is normal. Many of our autorickshaws and Pahari­ka buses departing from Rangamati left for Chattogram this morning."

Mohammad Yousuf, joint general secretary of the Rangamati Bus-Minibus Workers' Union, also confirmed the matter. He said that although traffic on the Chattogram route was normal, bus services on the Rangamati-Khagrachhari highway had been completely suspended due to the blockade.

Fizirikky Chakma, a resident of the Sapsari area, told Prothom Alo, "Vehicle movement on the Rangamati-Khagrachhari highway has been suspended since morning. I wanted to go to Rangamati market for some urgent work, but I could not go because no vehicles were available.

However, the blockade has not affected waterways, said Biswajit De, a lineman of the Rangamati Launch Owners' Association. He told Prothom Alo that launch services on Kaptai Lake in Rangamati were operating normally.

Rangamati Kotwali police station Inspector (Investigation) Mohammad Mokhlesur Rahman said no untoward incidents had been reported anywhere so far in connection with the blockade.

In Khagrachhari, protesters staged demonstrations by burning tyres on roads in the Chengi Bridge and Swanirbhar areas of the town, the Agricultural Research area on the Khagrachhari-Dighinala road, and the Jorabridge area of Guimara on the Chattogram-Khagrachhari highway. Trees were felled to block the road in the Sapmara area of the Chattogram-Khagrachhari highway. A few autorickshaws were seen operating in different parts of the town. Night buses arriving from Dhaka early in the morning reached Khagrachhari under police escort.

Khagrachhari police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Mohammad Kai Kyslu said the night buses arriving from Dhaka had been brought to Khagrachhari under police escort. Some buses were delayed and were in Ramgarh. They had been asked to reach Khagrachhari after noon. Pickets had attempted to create disorder by burning tyres at several locations in the town. Law enforcement personnel went to the sites and chased them away. The situation remained calm so far, he said.

Speaking about the overall situation during the blockade, Ushatan Chakma, president of the Chhatra-Janatar Sangram Parishad, said, "We are making every effort to carry out the blockade programme peacefully. However, law enforcement personnel obstructed our members while they were picketing in the Betbunia area."

Asked about the situation in Sajek, Sajek police station OC Tofazzal Hossain said army and police patrols had been intensified there. No reports of picketing had been received, but no vehicles were operating either.

The blockade was announced in a press release signed by Nirmal Chakma, organising secretary of the Chhatra-Janatar Sangram Parishad, on Thursday afternoon. The release sought cooperation from democratic and progressive organisations in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, as well as transport owners' and workers' organisations in Khagrachhari and Rangamati. Ambulances, fire service vehicles, vehicles carrying emergency medicine supplies and journalists' vehicles have been exempted from the blockade.

According to local sources, the Chhatra-Janatar Sangram Parishad is primarily a UPDF-supported organisation. However, a UPDF member denied the claim, saying that the organisation was not supported by them.

Earlier, on Wednesday, the Sajek Public Rights Protection Committee and the Sajek Karbari Association announced an indefinite blockade of the Sajek tourist road over three demands. This is the third round of blockades called by the two organisations. One of their key demands is the removal of armed members of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti (JSS), supported by Santu Larma, from the Sajek area.

However, the JSS has denied the allegation. Sajeeb Chakma, the organisation's information and publicity secretary, told Prothom Alo, "Such fabricated allegations are being made to divert attention from the long-standing oppression and harassment of ordinary people in Sajek by armed UPDF members."

After Sajek Gon-Odhikar Rokkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association announced the blockade last Wednesday, the Rangamati district administration temporarily closed the Sajek tourist destination, citing security concerns. A public notice signed by Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi said Sajek Valley would remain closed until further notice. Tourists were also instructed to leave Sajek safely by 4:00pm on Thursday.

Following the directive, tourists began leaving Sajek on Thursday morning. However, on their way back, they faced obstruction from protesters in the Ujo Bazar area.

The tourist convoy resumed its journey after law enforcement personnel removed the protesters from the road. Gunfire broke out at around 11:00am. Law enforcement agencies said armed UPDF members had opened fire targeting tourists and law enforcement personnel. The UPDF, however, denied the allegation.

Amid the tension, 2,933 tourists stranded in Sajek were escorted by security forces to Khagrachhari town at around 1:00pm on Thursday.

item.title: Teacher shortages put pressure on government schools
item.description:
At around 11am on a sunny morning, students at Abul Bashar Government Primary School in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur were playing in the corridor while classrooms remained empty. Asked why classes were not taking place, some children said their teacher was absent.
Similar scenes were observed during visits to several government primary schools in Mohammadpur and Agargaon, where teacher shortages and large class sizes raised concerns about regular classroom teaching.
The pressure is reflected in school-level figures. Siddique Miah Obaitonik RPS has 308 students and only five teachers, an average of about 62 students per teacher. Government records indicate that the school should have at least eight teachers.
Rebeka Sultana, headteacher of Siddique Miah Primary School, told Dhaka Tribune: “Yes, there were three vacant posts. But after the recent assistant teacher recruitment process, they will be filled.”
At Jobeda Khatun RPS, six teachers serve 254 students, or around 42 students per teacher. Badshamia Government Primary School has 542 students and 14 teachers, averaging about 39 students per teacher.
Agargaon Taltola Government Primary School has 635 students and 18 teachers. Headteacher Nasrin Akter said the student-teacher ratio was around 37:1, while the school also faced a shortage of classrooms.
“We have a shortage of rooms. If the second-phase development project is implemented, this problem will also be resolved,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
Teachers said their workload extends beyond classroom teaching. Schools open at 7:30am, classes begin at 8am and continue until 2pm, with each class lasting 50 minutes. Teachers must also send photographs confirming their attendance to a designated group.
A teacher, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “Taking classes for such long hours while handling various other responsibilities is difficult to describe. On top of that, we have to deal with a lot of administrative work every day. And then there is also a shortage of manpower and classrooms.”
Data from the Integrated Primary Education Information Management System (IPEMIS) show that 23 primary schools under the Mohammadpur Thana education office have 7,447 students and 260 teachers. Staffing pressure varies across schools, with some having considerably more students per teacher than others.
The shortage of permanent headteachers is a nationwide concern. According to the Directorate of Primary Education, 27,734 of the country’s 65,553 headteacher posts are vacant.
When a headteacher’s post remains vacant, an assistant teacher may have to handle administrative responsibilities alongside regular classes. These duties include maintaining records, submitting reports, managing attendance and coordinating school activities, leaving less time for teaching.
Mohammadpur Thana Education Officer Nayer Sultana acknowledged that some schools in the area did not have headteachers. She expressed hope that the problem would ease as recruitment and deployment progressed.
The government has recommended 14,384 candidates for assistant teacher posts. However, not all completed the appointment process within the stipulated period. A significant number of assistant teacher vacancies are also expected to remain even after the new recruits join.
Meanwhile, officials said the government planned to fill vacant headteacher posts through promotion. The appointment process had been delayed by legal complications and litigation, but a court ruling earlier this year paved the way for recruitment to resume.
State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj said the government was addressing teacher shortages through recruitment, promotions and a new teacher policy covering training, deployment and professional development.
He said the process of filling headteacher posts had begun and stressed that teachers should receive training before entering classrooms.
Government secondary schools face similar pressure, with vacancies affecting both overall staffing and the availability of teachers for specific subjects.
Of 15,293 sanctioned assistant teacher posts across 702 government secondary schools, 2,842 were vacant in the latest reported figures, accounting for around 18.6%. Another 383 headteacher posts and 249 assistant headteacher posts were unfilled.
At Shahid Monu Mia Government High School, Dhaka Tribune found seven teachers, including the headteacher, serving around 400 students.
Acting headteacher Md Delwar Hossain said the shortage of teachers in specific subjects meant existing teachers had to take five to six classes a day, while the headteacher also had to teach.
“Many subject teachers are not available. This is how we are running the school,” he said.
Vacancies are particularly pronounced in several subject areas. According to the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), government secondary schools have 319 of 1,020 social science posts, 253 of 786 business studies posts, 252 of 854 biology posts and 210 of 881 physical science posts vacant.
Vacancies also include 452 Bangla, 256 religious studies, 155 fine arts and 173 physical education posts.
Educationists say shortages of subject specialists may be affecting students’ Secondary School Certificate (SSC) results.
DSHE Director General Prof Khan Moynuddin Al Mahmud Sohel said teacher shortages had made school operations difficult.
He said recruitment delays under the Bangladesh Public Service Commission’s non-cadre system had prolonged the crisis, adding that the issue had been raised with the Education Ministry.
Teacher shortages are compounded by weaknesses in classroom practices and academic management.
Recently published data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS) show that only 6,317, or 47.99%, of the 13,164 teachers in government secondary schools had professional training.
An inspection by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education, conducted between April and June, covered 5,431 schools and monitored classroom activities at 2,747 of them.
The findings showed that learning materials were not aligned with lesson content in 57% of the schools monitored, while 52% did not properly maintain continuous assessment records.
Experts say recruitment and training initiatives may ease the pressure, but the challenge extends beyond the number of appointments. Schools need teachers in the subjects they teach, permanent academic leadership and working conditions that allow teachers to focus on students rather than carry an excessive administrative burden.
Professor Mohammad Mujibur Rahman of the University of Dhaka’s Institute of Education and Research told Dhaka Tribune that teacher shortages often received less attention than equipment and classroom technology.
“Teachers are the ones who create smart students,” he said, calling for greater focus on filling vacancies and supporting teachers.
Emeritus Professor Manzoor Ahmed told Dhaka Tribune: “Filling vacant posts alone will not be enough. A comprehensive plan is needed to determine how many teachers are required in each subject, how they should be recruited and deployed, and how classroom teaching quality can be improved.”

item.title: 3 killed as bus plunges into ditch on Dhaka-Mawa Expressway
item.description:
Three people were killed and 16 others injured when a bus plunged into a roadside ditch on the Dhaka-Mawa Expressway in Sreenagar upazila of Munshiganj district early Saturday.
One of the deceased was identified as Rakonuzzaman Ranju, 55, of Chuadanga district, while the identities of the other two could not be known immediately.
The accident occurred around 3:18am in the Hasara area when the Dhaka-bound bus of ‘Darshana Paribahan’ from Chuadanga, smashed through the roadside railing and plunged into a ditch as its driver lost control while overtaking a covered van at high speed, leaving three killed on the spot and 16 others injured, said Muhammad Shafiqul Islam, deputy assistant director of Munshiganj Fire Service and Civil Defence.
On information, two firefighting units of Sreenagar Fire Station rushed to the spot and rescued 11 injured passengers from the bus before taking them to Sreenagar Upazila Health Complex.
Five others received first aid at the spot.

item.title: Messi receives top Spanish award from heir to throne
item.description:
Lionel Messi received Spain's most prestigious sports award on Friday in recognition of his glittering career and his work for disadvantaged children's access to health and education.
The Argentine forward, 39, was named winner of the Princess of Asturias Award for Sports in June, with the jury hailing "the most successful footballer of all time" and his social work.
Dozens of fans wearing Argentina football shirts cheered and chanted Messi's name as he arrived to the sound of bagpipes and drums at the ceremony in Oviedo, capital of the northern Spanish region of Asturias.
Messi collected a formal roll of parchment from Princess Leonor, the heir to the Spanish throne after whom the awards are named, who lauded his "unique career".
"He turned the extraordinary into routine by reading the game and deciding on the most effective option in fractions of a second, while respecting the collective essence above ego," Leonor said.
One of the greatest footballers of all time, Messi has won eight Ballon d'Or titles, a World Cup and dozens of trophies at club level.
He spent 21 years at Barcelona where he played in a side that dominated Spain and Europe under Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique.
After leaving the Catalan club in 2021, Messi spent two years at French giants Paris Saint-Germain and currently plays for Inter Miami in MLS.
Argentina's all-time top goalscorer, assist provider and caps holder called time on his international career earlier this year after losing the World Cup final to Spain in New Jersey.
"The most important thing is to know how to lose and how to win," Messi told an event with children in Oviedo on Thursday, saying that attitude was "fundamental" in football.
Founded in 1981, the Princess of Asturias Awards are the most prestigious in the Spanish-speaking world and come with prize money of 50,000 euros ($56,000).
They encompass the arts, sciences and sports and are handed out annually in honour of efforts to improve human coexistence, solidarity and global cooperation.
British author Julian Barnes, trailblazing US astronaut Christina Koch and punk star Patti Smith were among the other winners who received their prize on Friday.
Previous winners of the sports award include tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal, marathon record-breaker Eliud Kipchoge and US skier Lindsey Vonn.

item.title: Bayern coach Kompany in hospital after collapsing
item.description:
Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital by an emergency medical team on Friday after collapsing during training, the club said.
"Vincent Kompany had to seek medical attention on Friday after collapsing during a training session with FC Bayern's reserve team," Bayern said on their website.
"Kompany is undergoing thorough examinations at the hospital and will remain under medical care."
Kompany, the 40-year-old former Manchester City defender, missed training and a press conference on Tuesday ahead of Bayern's Champions League draw against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena.
"I caught a pretty nasty virus last week, and of course I didn't listen to my body -- and then at some point my body just said, 'enough is enough!'" Kompany said after the Arsenal game.
On Friday, Bayern's sporting director Max Eberl said the health of their coach "is our top priority".
"We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure he recovers quickly. Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical care and support, as well as all the time he needs. His coaching staff, whom we trust completely, will take over his duties."
English assistant coach Aaron Danks took training and handled the press conference ahead of the Arsenal game.
"It affected his legs at times; he was experiencing some pain. It's just a virus. He needs rest," Danks said on Tuesday.
"The most important thing we're encouraging him to do right now is to rest and take as much time as he needs—no matter how long that may be."
Bundesliga leaders Bayern visit Freiburg, who are third in the table, on Saturday.
Their next Champions League match is on November 3 in Madrid against Atletico.
The Spanish club posted their best wishes on social media.
"We wish you a speedy recovery. We hope to see you here in Madrid, on the bench, in a few days," wrote the Spanish club adding a heart emoji.
Kompany, a centre back, started his career with Anderlecht in his native Brussels. He moved to Hamburg and then to Manchester City as one of the club's last signings before the Abu Dhabi takeover in 2008.
He went on to play 360 games for the club, where he was also captain for eight season as the team became the dominant force in English football.
He played 89 times for Belgium and finished his playing career back at Anderlecht in 2019 where he was player-coach in the first of his three seasons in charge
He took over at Burnley in 2022, leading them to a Championship title in 2023 but the club was relegated the next season with their lowest ever points total.
Bayern, who had just endured a trophyless season and had been unable to persuade Thomas Tuchel to stay, sprung a surprise by paying Burnley to sign Kompany as manager in 2024.
He led the club two the Bundesliga title each of his first two seasons and to a German Cup in 2026. After six games, Bayern lead the table this season on goal difference. In 74 Bundesliga games under Kompany, Bayern have won 57 and lost three.
Kompany completed an MBA at Manchester Business School in 2018.

"He is always friendly, open, and approachable. Yet, he knows exactly what he wants and how he wants it done on the pitch,"

item.title: Summer Athletics 2026: Imranur, Shirin claim 100m gold
item.description:
Bangladesh Navy’s sprinters Imranur Rahman and Shirin Akter dominated the men’s and women’s 100 metres respectively in the 18th Koko National Summer Athletics competition, as fresh promises were made to improve athletes’ accommodation, nutrition and transport facilities.
On the first day of the competition held at National Stadium on Friday, Imranur clocked 10.53 seconds to win the men’s 100m gold, finishing ahead of his fellow Navy sprinter Mohammad Ismail, who took silver in 10.67 seconds. Army’s Tarek Rahman claimed bronze in 10.73 seconds.
Shirin won the women’s 100m title in 12.08 seconds. Army’s Sharifa Khatun finished second in 12.23 seconds, while Navy’s Sumaiya Dewan took third place in 12.33 seconds.
Shirin credited her success to the support of her teammates, coach and sporting organisations.
“Alhamdulillah, by the infinite mercy of Allah, it feels wonderful to finish first,” she said after winning the coveted gold.
She acknowledged the contributions of coach Abdullah Hel Kafi, Bangladesh Navy, Bangladesh Krira Shikkha Protishtan (BKSP), Bangladesh Athletics Federation and Bangladesh Olympic Association to her achievement.
Shirin also expressed hope that the performance would boost her preparations for the upcoming South Asian competitions.
Meanwhile, Imranur stressed the need to improve facilities for athletes, saying initiatives were being taken to address their accommodation, food, nutritional and transport needs.
Efforts are also being made to encourage more athletes from district-level competitions to participate, with greater coordination among the relevant organisations.
Organisers expect improved accommodation, nutritious meals and transport support to encourage wider participation and help identify emerging talent across the country.
Earlier, President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir formally inaugurated the meet as the chief guest.
State Minister for Youth and Sports Md. Aminul Haque addressed the event as a special guest while Bangladesh Athletics Federation (BAF) general secretary Advocate Ali Imam Tapan delivered the welcome address with BAF President Mohammad Abdullah Zaber in the chair.

item.title: Measles: Beyond the blame game
item.description:
Official data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) recorded as of October 23, 2026, presents a heartbreaking reality for our nation: The combined measles death toll has reached 1,214 fatalities.
With nationwide suspected cases surging past 218,870 during the same reporting window, public anger and frustration are entirely justified.
When parents lose their children to a disease that is supposed to be fully preventable by routine immunization, asking hard questions is not just right, it is necessary.
If there has been institutional negligence, administrative complacency, or a lack of absolute sincerity in rolling out and monitoring proper vaccination coverage, those responsible must be held strictly accountable through transparent investigations and exemplary punishment.
Public trust in our national health programs depends on zero tolerance for official dereliction of duty.
Yet, while safeguarding vaccination integrity is our absolute first line of defense, fixing this crisis requires looking at the complete picture.
The frustration on the streets must be matched by a deeper understanding of the multi-layered vulnerabilities that allow this virus to devastate our communities.
To understand why this outbreak has taken such a devastating toll, we must examine who is being affected.
While the official DGHS divisional data shows that transmission spans all eight divisions, the outbreak burden is heavily concentrated in Dhaka and Chittagong, which together account for over 60% of nationwide cases and deaths, alongside significant mortality in Barisal, Sylhet, and Mymensingh.
Surveillance patterns and media reports point toward a clear socio-economic reality: The vast majority of severe hospitalizations and fatalities occur among children in congested urban slums, informal settlements, and hard-to-reach riverine regions.
These parents face grinding daily economic struggles and limited educational access, meaning missed routine Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) doses are often exacerbated by systemic barriers and logistical failures.
However, focusing solely on vaccination gaps misses a critical biological reality. Measles severity and mortality are intimately tied to a child's baseline nutritional status.
Persistent food inflation forces vulnerable families to cut back on high-quality animal proteins, such as eggs, milk, poultry, and meat which are essential for providing bioavailable iron, zinc, and Vitamin A.
A malnourished child possesses compromised cell-mediated immunity; when the measles virus strikes, their depleted defense systems fail to contain it, turning a manageable childhood infection into a fatal crisis.
For the children who survive the acute phase of measles, a hidden and insidious danger remains: "Immune amnesia."
Medical science demonstrates that the measles virus systematically wipes out a significant portion of the body's immune memory cells.
In the months and years following recovery, these children essentially "forget" how to fight off everyday bacterial and viral pathogens they previously resisted, leaving them perilously vulnerable to secondary infections.
Overcoming this requires structured post-recovery care, immediate Vitamin A supplementation, and sustained, protein-rich diets to help rebuild their shattered immune architecture.
Though measles is a human-to-human virus rather than a zoonotic pathogen, managing its threat effectively requires evaluating how broader environmental, agricultural, and socio-economic systems intersect with public health.
A One Health framework recognizes that human immunity and disease transmission do not exist in clinical isolation:
Toward collective action
If we are to prevent future tragedies and break the cycle of recurring health crises, we must combine unsparing accountability for vaccination delivery with comprehensive structural reform:
Measles is entirely preventable. The true measure of our public health resilience is not how many hospital beds we scramble to arrange during an emergency, but how strictly we enforce accountability, maintain flawless vaccination coverage, and protect our children through robust nutrition and an integrated defense.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

item.title: The United Nations at 81: The world still waits for action
item.description:
On October 24 2026, the world observes “United Nations Day” amid a profound test of international cooperation. Wars threaten civilians, geopolitical rivalries obstruct collective action, human rights remain unevenly protected, and climate change disproportionately affects the most vulnerable.
Established in the aftermath of WWII, the United Nations (UN) embodied a historic ambition: To prevent future conflicts through dialogue, diplomacy and collective action.
Eighty-one years after its Charter entered into force, that ambition remains indispensable. Yet, the widening gap between its founding ideals and present realities raises a critical question: Can the UN still deliver on its promise?
Although every member state has an equal vote in the General Assembly, influence remains unequal, particularly in the Security Council. The challenge is not whether the world needs the UN, but whether it can become more effective, representative, and accountable.
The Security Council’s ability to act decisively is frequently constrained by geopolitical rivalries and the veto power of its five permanent members. When strategic interests prevail over collective responsibility, the credibility of the international system suffers -- and civilians pay the price. Families lose their homes, children are deprived of education, and millions are forced to flee.
Peace must mean more than the absence of fighting. It must allow people to return home safely, live without fear, and rebuild their lives with dignity.
Greater representation for underrepresented regions and meaningful restraint in the use of the veto when mass atrocities occur would strengthen the organization’s legitimacy. Such reforms, however, require genuine political will from influential member states.
Rebuilding trust in multilateralism
Rising nationalism, political polarization, and declining public confidence are straining international cooperation. Some governments view international agreements as constraints on sovereignty, while others question whether multilateral institutions apply their principles consistently.
Restoring trust requires fairness, transparency, and measurable results. Powerful nations must accept the same accountability they demand of others.
These divisions were evident during the 81st session of the General Assembly. On September 23, Argentine President Javier Milei described the UN as an “ineffective organization” and its officials as “arrogant parasites.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, by contrast, called for Security Council reform and the abolition of the veto.
Restrictions driven by political considerations can undermine humanitarian assistance and essential services. The answer is not weaker multilateralism, but more credible and dependable cooperation, supported by transparency and honoured commitments.
Pandemics, climate change, and cyber threats demonstrate that no country can adequately address major global challenges alone. Responsible multilateralism serves national interests as well as humanity’s shared interests.
Human rights must be universal
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights established a common standard of dignity, freedom, and equality. Yet its principles remain unevenly upheld.
Governments sometimes invoke sovereignty to deflect criticism, while surveillance, online censorship, and digital repression create new threats to fundamental freedoms.
The UN’s credibility depends on defending human rights consistently, without political selectivity. Civilian protection, freedom of expression, and equality before the law must never become bargaining chips in geopolitical alliances.
Credible investigations and accountability for serious violations are essential to ensuring that justice does not depend on political influence.
Sustainable development requires global solidarity
The 2030 Agenda and its 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a shared framework for tackling poverty, inequality, inadequate healthcare, educational disparities, and environmental degradation. Yet, economic shocks, debt distress, and climate change continue to obstruct progress.
Communities that have contributed least to environmental pressures often possess the fewest resources to withstand their consequences.
For Bangladesh, international cooperation is vital to securing affordable and predictable climate finance, accessible technology, capacity-building, and fairer economic arrangements.
Reforming the global financial architecture and addressing unsustainable debt must remain priorities. Wealthier nations must also translate their climate commitments into tangible action.
Nevertheless, international assistance alone cannot guarantee development. Effective national leadership, sound governance, and accountability are equally important.
The UN should support national priorities while ensuring that development reaches communities most at risk of being left behind.
The 81st session’s priority theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” captures the challenge. Trust must be earned through tangible improvements in people’s lives. The UN needs stronger coordination among its agencies and greater accountability for results.
Responsibility is shared. An organization established by governments cannot overcome international divisions without their cooperation. Civil society, young people, and journalists also play vital roles in holding institutions accountable and translating global commitments into local action.
Bangladesh and other developing countries should build coalitions, advocate fairer international rules, and ensure that vulnerable communities have a meaningful voice in global decision-making.
A renewed commitment
This day should prompt reflection on the distance between the world we aspire to build and the realities people experience.
The UN is far from perfect, but the need for a forum where nations can negotiate and cooperate remains undeniable. As UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih stated, “Peace must be measured not only by agreements signed, but by lives changed.”
At 81, the UN needs renewed commitment to its founding principles, meaningful institutional reform, and a willingness among member states to place humanity above narrow political interests.
Its success must be measured not by the resolutions it adopts, but by its ability to alleviate the suffering caused by war, protect human rights, expand opportunities for developing countries, and safeguard the planet for future generations.
The world needs a United Nations that does more than speak on behalf of all; it needs one that delivers for all.
Nicholas Biswas , is a media freelancer and recipient of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Media Award.

item.title: Sharing the streets
item.description:
Bringing Dhaka’s street food vendors under a formal registration system -- through the Bangladesh Safe Food Authority initiative starting on November 1 -- is a reasonable step towards improving food safety and recognizing a sector that has long operated informally.
While the authorities prepare to introduce mandatory registration, however, they must also ensure that the process offers vendors genuine protection rather than another reason for them to fear harassment.
The initiative has the potential to make food safety oversight more effective for both traders and consumers by identifying vendors, providing hygiene training, and establishing clear standards. Free initial registration is also a welcome decision, particularly for people whose livelihoods depend on small daily earnings.
However, registration alone cannot address the difficulties street vendors face: Many continue to work under the threat of extortion and arbitrary eviction, often without access to designated spaces where they can operate without obstructing pedestrians.
A certificate will not amount to much if vendors remain vulnerable to illegal demands or are removed from their workplaces without clear rules or due process.
The authorities must therefore treat registration as part of a broader policy for managing street commerce. Local administrations need to establish designated vending areas, communicate regulations clearly, and ensure that enforcement is consistent and transparent. Vendors should also be made aware of necessary documentation, expected standards, and clear, formal ways to report harassment.
At the same time, food safety cannot be treated as a mere formality. Vendors should receive practical guidance and reasonable opportunities to meet hygiene requirements, while those who repeatedly disregard essential standards are held accountable.
Dhaka needs cleaner, safer, and better-organized streets, but this cannot come at the cost of livelihoods without offering workable alternatives.
At the end of the day, whether this formal registration system is used to support compliance, protect small traders, and regulate public spaces fairly or simply add another layer of bureaucracy remains to be seen.

item.title: For meaningful transport overhaul
item.description:
However, the real test of this initiative will be whether it leads to meaningful improvements in how buses operate, rather than remaining a cosmetic exercise.
For years, Dhaka’s commuters have endured overcrowding, reckless driving, competition for passengers, unsafe boarding and disembarking, and buses that are poorly maintained.
These problems cannot be solved through superficial changes alone. Even after these planned reforms, if buses continue to stop wherever their drivers please, compete dangerously with other vehicles, and disregard traffic rules, little will have changed for the people who depend on it every day.
This is not to dismiss the value of the initiative. Visible changes can help establish a new standard, and a phased approach may be more practical than attempting to overhaul the entire system overnight.
But such measures must be accompanied by stronger regulation, regular fitness inspections, disciplined route management, and consistent enforcement of traffic laws. Bus owners and operators must also be held accountable for the conduct of their drivers and the safety of their vehicles.
Equally important is improving the experience of passengers. Properly designated stops, safer boarding facilities, reliable services, and reasonable fares are essential to making public transport more dependable.
Workers in the sector must also be brought into the reform process, with clear rules and incentives that discourage reckless competition.
Dhaka cannot afford to keep revisiting the same problems through successive rounds of cosmetic change. The new colours can be a welcome first step, but they must mark the beginning of a sustained effort to reform public transport.
Ultimately, commuters need buses that are safe, reliable, and accountable -- not merely buses that look different.

item.title: Anee: Collective social movement needed to build better society
item.description:
Water Resources Minister and BNP Joint Secretary General Md Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee on Friday called for a united social movement to protect people's dignity and build a better society, saying the people had suffered significant losses over the past 17 years and did not want to lose anything more.
He made the call while addressing a meeting organised by Life Line Welfare Organization at Ayesha High School field in Totakhil under Chandraganj upazila of Lakshmipur.
Anee urged people to remain united against social problems and work collectively to build a better society, noting that the country had been regained through struggle and sacrifice.
"Do not issue threats of a one-point movement; there is no benefit in making such threats," he said, adding that the BNP had emerged from the streets through movements and struggles and would not be intimidated.
He alleged that Jamaat-e-Islami had colluded with the Awami League and enforced strikes and blockades for 172 days in 1996.
The minister also described Islami Chhatra Shibir as a clandestine organisation that had operated at various universities before August 5, urging people to remain vigilant.
Criticising opposition parties, Anee alleged that they were obstructing the government outside Parliament despite delivering eloquent speeches inside the House.
Political parties, he said, should focus on national and social development rather than confining their activities to rallies and meetings.
Anee also called for collective efforts to counter religious misinterpretations, misinformation and drug abuse, warning that those involved in such activities would not be spared regardless of their influence.
Later, he distributed sewing machines among women.

item.title: Five killed, seven injured in separate road accidents in Faridpur
item.description:
Five people, including a mother and her son, were killed and at least seven others injured in two separate road accidents in Faridpur on Friday.
In the first incident, a sand-laden truck overturned onto an autorickshaw and a private car in the Tetultala area of Kanaipur on the Dhaka-Khulna highway around 3:30pm, killing Sumi Begum, 32, and her son Shaon, 7. Four passengers of the private car were injured.
Senior Station Officer of Faridpur Fire Service Sribas Baroi said the truck reportedly lost control and overturned, causing the accident. The injured were receiving treatment at hospital.
In another accident, three people were killed when a Magura-bound ambulance collided head-on with a Dhaka-bound King Fisher bus near Arkandi Bridge in Madhukhali upazila around noon.
One of the deceased was identified as Rabbi, 21, while the identities of the other two could not be immediately known.
The victims were reportedly students from Magura Sadar who were returning home after attending a Red Crescent blood donation programme in Faridpur.
The injured were taken to nearby hospitals, with two later referred to Faridpur Medical College Hospital for better treatment.
Officer-in-Charge of Karimpur Highway Police Station, said three people were killed in the bus-ambulance collision. Police were working to identify the deceased and determine the cause of the accident.
